answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Chapter IV of Woolf’s 1929 essay A Room of One’s Own, where she gives this line as the imagined defiant thought of a woman writer determined to keep working despite being shut out of libraries and colleges.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 28 September 1929 (Hogarth Press, London; Harcourt, Brace & Co., New York)
Expanded from two lectures Woolf gave at Newnham College and Girton College, Cambridge, in October 1928

source.excerpt: One must have been something of a firebrand to say to oneself, Oh, but they can’t buy literature too. Literature is open to everybody. I refuse to allow you, Beadle though you are, to turn me off the grass. Lock up your libraries if you like; but there is no gate, no lock, no bolt that you can set upon the freedom of my mind.
trail: First delivered as two lectures at Newnham College and Girton College, Cambridge, in October 1928, then published as A Room of One’s Own ↗ by the Hogarth Press in September 1929.
The line appears in Chapter IV, where Woolf imagines the defiant thought a woman writer of 1828 needed in order to keep working — wording confirmed against Wikisource’s transcription of Chapter IV ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ independently sources the same line to page 90 of the 1929 edition, listing it among Woolf’s verified quotations rather than her misattributed ones.
A printed edition of the essay is preserved as a digitized scan in the Internet Archive ↗.
source.excerptNote: Woolf presents the line as the defiant private thought of an imagined 1828 woman writer — the wording is her own composition in the essay's narrating voice, not a quotation attributed to a real historical person.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf was a leading figure of English literary modernism, known for novels such as Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. In A Room of One’s Own (1929) — expanded from lectures she gave to women students at Cambridge — she argued that a woman needs money and privacy to write, a text that became a foundational work of feminist literary criticism.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Woolf casts the line as the inner monologue of an imagined 1828 woman writer, using free indirect speech to dramatize the defiance needed to keep writing despite the snubs, closed libraries, and denied prizes that greeted women's ambitions.

The essay grew out of two lectures Woolf gave to female Cambridge undergraduates in October 1928 — at a time when Cambridge did not yet grant women full degrees — and was published the following year as a six-chapter book arguing that a woman needs money and privacy of her own in order to write fiction.
